prompt: What are the two primary viewpoints or definitions of an Operating System?

options.text: As an Extended Machine (providing clean abstractions) and as a Resource Manager (allocating CPU, memory, I/O)
As a compiler and as a hardware assembler
As an application software and as a database management system
As a networking protocol and as a web server

explanation: From top-down, an OS is an Extended Machine (virtual machine) shielding users from raw hardware complexity. From bottom-up, it is a Resource Manager arbitrating competing requests for CPU, memory, and devices.

prompt: What is the primary operational goal of a general-purpose Operating System for personal computers?

options.text: User convenience and ease of use, with good performance
Maximizing CPU utilization to 100% at the cost of responsiveness
Eliminating all user interaction
Running only one single task indefinitely

explanation: For personal computers, the primary goal is user convenience. For mainframes and supercomputers, the primary goal is efficient hardware utilization.

prompt: What was a major disadvantage of early 'Serial Processing' systems (1940s-1950s)?

options.text: Substantial setup time and idle CPU while operators mounted tapes, cards, and printed outputs
Too many background threads running simultaneously
Complex virtual memory page faults
Excessive internet bandwidth consumption

explanation: In early serial processing, users signed up for machine slots. Setup times for loading compilers, source tapes, and punch cards kept the expensive CPU idle for most of the session.

prompt: What does SPOOLing stand for in operating systems?

options.text: Simultaneous Peripheral Operations On-Line
Serial Peripheral Output Oriented Line
Synchronous Program Over Operating Link
System Process Optimization Online Log

explanation: SPOOLing (Simultaneous Peripheral Operations On-Line) uses high-speed disk storage as a buffer between slow I/O devices (like card readers and printers) and the high-speed CPU.

prompt: What is the core difference between a Batch Operating System and a Multiprogrammed Operating System?

options.text: Multiprogramming keeps multiple jobs in memory simultaneously to keep the CPU busy during I/O delays
Batch systems can switch tasks in milliseconds interactively
Multiprogramming only works on single-core 8-bit CPUs
Batch systems require no storage devices

explanation: In a batch system, only one job executes at a time. In multiprogramming, multiple jobs reside in memory; whenever the active job waits for I/O, the OS switches the CPU to another job, maximizing CPU utilization.

prompt: What is the defining characteristic of a 'Time-Sharing' (Multitasking) Operating System?

options.text: Rapid switching of the CPU among multiple interactive users using small time slices (quanta)
Running jobs strictly one after another in batches
Elimination of scheduling queues
Dedicated CPU for each individual user on separate motherboards

explanation: Time-sharing allocates small slices of CPU time (e.g., 10-100 ms) to each user or process, providing the illusion of simultaneous, interactive execution.

prompt: What is the primary constraint that characterizes a 'Hard Real-Time' Operating System?

options.text: Strict deadlines that must be guaranteed without fail, where missing a deadline causes catastrophic failure
Pleasant user graphics with high frame rates
High throughput over hours
Low cost hardware compatibility

explanation: In hard real-time systems (e.g., automotive ABS, pacemakers, avionics), missing a deadline constitutes total system failure. In soft real-time (e.g., video streaming), missing a deadline degrades quality without catastrophe.

prompt: How does modern hardware enforce protection between the Operating System and user programs?

options.text: Through dual-mode CPU operation: User Mode (restricted) and Kernel / Supervisor Mode (privileged)
By encrypting user source code with AES-256
By physically disconnecting memory chips
By disabling the system clock interrupt

explanation: CPUs include a mode bit (0 = kernel mode, 1 = user mode). Privileged instructions (I/O, halt, interrupt control, memory register modification) can only execute in kernel mode.

prompt: Which of the following operations is classified as a 'privileged instruction' executable ONLY in Kernel Mode?

options.text: Direct hardware I/O instructions (in/out) and modifying memory limit registers
Adding two integer registers
Performing a conditional jump (jump if zero)
Calling a user-defined function

explanation: Hardware I/O, altering memory management registers, disabling interrupts, and clearing the CPU halt flag are privileged instructions to prevent user programs from compromising system integrity.

prompt: What hardware mechanism is used by a user application to request a service from the operating system kernel?

options.text: A System Call executed via a software interrupt or trap instruction
A direct jump to physical address 0x000000
A hardware reset button press
A compiler optimization directive

explanation: A system call executes a software interrupt or special CPU instruction (e.g., 'syscall' or 'int 0x80'), which safely switches the CPU from User Mode to Kernel Mode via the interrupt vector.

prompt: What is a 'trap' (or exception) in computer architecture?

options.text: A software-generated interrupt caused either by an error (divide by zero, invalid memory access) or a user system call request
A hardware failure in the power supply
An infinite loop in user code
A network packet drop

explanation: A trap is a synchronous software interrupt triggered by the executing CPU instruction itself, transferring control immediately to the kernel handler.

prompt: What is the fundamental architectural philosophy of a 'Microkernel' Operating System (e.g., Mach, QNX)?

options.text: Moving as many non-essential OS services as possible (file system, device drivers) out of the kernel into user-space servers
Putting all OS services, networking, and graphics into a single massive kernel binary
Eliminating all inter-process communication
Using only assembly language for the entire OS

explanation: A microkernel implements only bare minimum mechanisms (low-level memory, thread scheduling, and IPC) in kernel space. All other services run as isolated user-mode daemons, enhancing modularity and fault isolation.

prompt: What is the major performance trade-off associated with Microkernel architectures compared to Monolithic kernels?

options.text: Increased context switching and IPC message-passing overhead between user-space servers and the kernel
Lack of memory protection
Inability to run on 64-bit processors
Complete absence of device drivers

explanation: Because services like file systems and drivers run as separate user processes, every service request involves multiple user-to-kernel mode switches and IPC messages, introducing performance latency.

prompt: What is a 'Monolithic Kernel' architecture (e.g., traditional UNIX, Linux)?

options.text: An architecture where all core OS components (virtual memory, file systems, network stack, drivers) run together in a single kernel address space
An architecture with no kernel at all
An architecture designed exclusively for single-user microcomputers
An OS running entirely in BIOS ROM

explanation: In a monolithic kernel, all subsystems share the same kernel address space, enabling ultra-fast direct function calls between subsystems without IPC overhead.

prompt: What is the 'Layered Approach' to operating system design (e.g., THE multiprogramming system by Dijkstra)?

options.text: Structuring the OS as a hierarchy of layers (Layer 0 to N), where each layer is built solely on top of lower layers and provides services only to higher layers
Writing the OS in multiple programming languages
Splitting the hard drive into physical strata
Running multiple operating systems inside each other

explanation: The layered approach modularizes the OS into strictly ordered abstraction tiers: Layer 0 handles hardware, and Layer N provides user interfaces. Layer i can only invoke routines of Layer i-1.

prompt: Which system call is used in UNIX/Linux to create an exact duplicate clone of the calling process?

options.text: fork()
exec()
clone_thread()
spawn()

explanation: The fork() system call creates a new child process that is an exact duplicate of the parent process, sharing identical code, data, and environment up to the point of invocation.

prompt: What integer value does the fork() system call return to the newly created child process upon success?

options.text: The child's PID
The parent's PID

explanation: fork() returns 0 to the child process, returns the child's positive PID to the parent process, and returns -1 if the fork fails.

prompt: Which system call family replaces the current process memory image, code segment, and stack with a new program executable?

options.text: exec() (execl, execv, execvp)
fork()
wait()
exit()

explanation: The exec() family of system calls loads a new binary executable into the calling process address space, overwriting its text and data segments while retaining the same PID.

prompt: What is the purpose of the wait() system call in UNIX process management?

options.text: Suspends the parent process until one of its child processes terminates and collects its exit status
Pauses execution for a specified number of milliseconds
Waits for a network packet to arrive
Halts the CPU to save power

explanation: wait() blocks the calling parent until a child process changes state or finishes, retrieving the child's termination status code and allowing the OS to deallocate the child's PCB.

prompt: What is an 'interrupt vector' in operating system architecture?

options.text: An array of memory addresses where interrupt handler service routines (ISRs) are stored
A 3D coordinate vector for GPU rendering
A hardware wire connecting the keyboard to the monitor
A linked list of currently active process IDs

explanation: The interrupt vector table (IVT) contains pointers to specific Interrupt Service Routines (ISRs) indexed by the interrupt request (IRQ) number.

prompt: What is the purpose of the Timer Interrupt in a modern preemptive multitasking operating system?

options.text: To periodically regain CPU control for the kernel to enforce time quantum slices and prevent infinite user loops
To display the digital clock on the desktop taskbar
To synchronize system RAM with CPU clock frequency
To calculate the temperature of the CPU core

explanation: Hardware timers trigger periodic interrupts (e.g., every 10 ms), guaranteeing that the OS scheduler regains control to evaluate process priorities and enforce time-slicing.

prompt: Which of the following is NOT an operating system component?

options.text: Web Browser Application (Google Chrome, Firefox)
Process Scheduler
Virtual Memory Manager
File System Driver

explanation: Web browsers, text editors, and video players are user-level application software, distinct from the core operating system kernel.

prompt: What is a 'Bootstrap Loader' in computer initialization?

options.text: A small firmware program stored in ROM/UEFI that locates the OS kernel, loads it into RAM, and initiates system boot
A hardware tool used to assemble motherboard components
A compiler that converts C code to machine code
A user utility to clean cache files

explanation: The bootstrap program (BIOS/UEFI/GRUB) initializes hardware registers, memory controllers, and loads the kernel image from storage into main memory.

prompt: What is the state of the mode bit when an interrupt occurs while user code is executing?

options.text: Hardware hardware switches the mode bit from 1 (User) to 0 (Kernel) automatically
The mode bit remains 1 throughout
The mode bit is deleted
The CPU powers off

explanation: Hardware architecture automatically clears the mode bit to 0 (Kernel mode) upon receiving any interrupt or trap, ensuring the ISR runs with full privileges.

prompt: What does the exit() system call do?

options.text: Terminates the calling process, releasing its allocated memory, open file descriptors, and leaving an exit code for the parent
Suspends the process to disk
Restarts the computer immediately
Closes only the terminal window

explanation: exit() performs graceful process termination, deallocates resources, and notifies the parent process.

prompt: What is the primary benefit of Command Line Interpreters (Shells) like Bash or PowerShell?

options.text: Direct, scriptable, and expressive control over operating system operations and automation
They provide high-definition graphical animations
They eliminate the need for an operating system kernel
They make typing on keyboards unnecessary

explanation: Shells provide a command language interface enabling system administrators and developers to execute programs, pipe outputs, and automate workflows via scripts.

prompt: What is a 'hybrid kernel' (such as Windows NT and macOS XNU)?

options.text: A design combining monolithic performance (running drivers/GUI in kernel space) with microkernel modularity concepts
A kernel that runs without an electric power supply
A kernel written partially in Python and partially in HTML
A system that has no kernel space

explanation: Hybrid kernels maintain monolithic execution speed for performance-critical subsystems (graphics, networking) while adopting microkernel-like message structures and layered abstraction.

prompt: Which system call is used to read data from an open file descriptor in POSIX/UNIX?

options.text: read(fd, buffer, count)
write(fd, buffer, count)
open(filename, flags)
seek(fd, offset)

explanation: The read() system call reads up to 'count' bytes from file descriptor 'fd' into memory buffer 'buffer'.

prompt: What is 'graceful degradation' (fault tolerance) in distributed or multiprocessor operating systems?

options.text: The ability of the system to continue functioning proportionally even when one or more hardware components fail
A system crash where all data is immediately erased
Slowing down CPU speed to prevent overheating
Gradual fading of screen brightness on low battery

explanation: Fault-tolerant systems gracefully degrade performance when a failure occurs rather than experiencing total system shutdown.

prompt: What is an 'Asymmetric Multiprocessing' (AMP) system?

options.text: A multiprocessor architecture where a master CPU controls the operating system and delegates tasks to slave processors
A system where all CPUs are completely equal and share the same kernel code concurrently
A computer with one CPU and two monitors
A system that uses analog and digital circuits together

explanation: In AMP, a master-slave relationship exists: one master processor schedules tasks and runs OS code, while subordinate processors execute assigned user workloads.

prompt: What is 'Symmetric Multiprocessing' (SMP)?

options.text: An architecture where all processors are peers, and each processor runs a copy of the operating system kernel concurrently
A system where one CPU controls all other CPUs
A system where CPUs are located in different cities
A computer that only has graphics processors

explanation: In SMP, multiple identical CPUs share common physical memory and I/O buses, with any CPU capable of executing kernel code and user tasks concurrently.

prompt: What is a 'Clustered System' in operating systems?

options.text: A group of independent, interconnected computers (nodes) working together and sharing storage via a storage-area network (SAN)
A single CPU with multiple internal ALUs
A hard drive divided into multiple partitions
A set of user folders on a desktop

explanation: Clustering links separate server nodes over high-speed networks to provide high availability and load-balanced computational power.

prompt: What is the role of the 'Device Driver' in an operating system?

options.text: To provide a standardized software interface between the OS kernel and specific hardware peripheral controller registers
To design computer hardware chips
To clean physical dust from disk drives
To replace motherboard firmware

explanation: Device drivers bridge the hardware-specific command set of peripheral controllers with the standardized uniform I/O subsystem of the OS.

prompt: Which register in the CPU points to the memory address of the next instruction to be fetched and executed?

options.text: Program Counter (PC) / Instruction Pointer (IP)
Accumulator (ACC)
Stack Pointer (SP)
Status / Flags Register

explanation: The Program Counter holds the memory address of the next instruction in sequence to be executed.

prompt: What happens during a 'Cold Boot' vs a 'Warm Boot'?

options.text: Cold boot starts a computer from a completely powered-off state; warm boot restarts the system without cutting main power
Cold boot uses liquid nitrogen; warm boot uses fans
Cold boot only tests RAM; warm boot loads the BIOS
There is no technical difference

explanation: A cold boot executes full Power-On Self-Test (POST) from zero power, whereas a warm (soft) boot skips power cycling and hardware self-checks, simply reloading the OS.

prompt: What is the primary role of the BIOS/UEFI firmware during computer startup?

options.text: Performs POST (Power-On Self-Test), initializes basic hardware interfaces, and locates the bootable boot sector
Compiles C programs into assembly code
Runs antivirus scans on the hard drive
Acts as the desktop window manager

explanation: Firmware checks system hardware integrity (POST) and transfers control to the bootloader found on the designated boot drive.

prompt: What is 'Memory Protection' enforced by the operating system using Base and Limit registers?

options.text: Ensures that a user process can only access physical memory within its designated range (Base <= Address < Base + Limit)
Locks RAM with physical security keys
Encrypts all memory contents with passwords
Prevents memory chips from overheating

explanation: Hardware base and limit registers define the legal physical address boundaries for a process. Any access outside these registers raises a hardware trap (segmentation violation).

prompt: What is an 'Operating System Service' for Information Maintenance?

options.text: System calls that retrieve or set system time, date, process attributes, and hardware configuration metadata
Formatting the hard drive to factory settings
Running spreadsheet calculations
Installing user video games

explanation: Information maintenance system calls include getpid(), time(), date(), and sysinfo() to inspect system state.

prompt: Which system call is used to create a new, empty file or rewrite an existing file in UNIX?

options.text: creat() / open() with O_CREAT flag
delete()
truncate()
copy()

explanation: creat() or open(path, O_CREAT | O_WRONLY | O_TRUNC, mode) creates a new file entry in the directory system.

prompt: Why does the OS kernel reside in the upper portion of virtual address space in modern operating systems?

options.text: To allow seamless context switching into kernel mode without having to swap page directory tables
Because kernel code must always be stored on CD-ROMs
To prevent physical RAM from being filled up
Because lower addresses cannot execute machine code

explanation: Mapping the kernel into the upper virtual address space of every user process allows system calls and interrupts to transition to kernel code instantly without requiring costly TLB flushes.

prompt: What is the POSIX standard in operating systems?

options.text: Portable Operating System Interface: an IEEE standard defining APIs for software compatibility across UNIX variants
A proprietary Microsoft programming language
A hardware protocol for serial mice
An open-source graphics editor

explanation: POSIX (Portable Operating System Interface) ensures that source code written for one compliant operating system (e.g., Linux) compiles and runs on others (e.g., macOS, BSD).

prompt: What is a 'Virtual Machine' (VM) managed by a Hypervisor (Type-1 or Type-2)?

options.text: An isolated software emulation of a complete physical computer system capable of running its own guest operating system
A web browser running an online game
A video card benchmark tool
A compressed zip folder containing code

explanation: A hypervisor virtualizes underlying hardware, allowing multiple guest operating systems to execute simultaneously in isolated virtual environments.

prompt: What is the difference between a Type-1 (Bare-Metal) Hypervisor and a Type-2 (Hosted) Hypervisor?

options.text: Type-1 runs directly on raw physical hardware; Type-2 runs as an application on top of an existing host operating system
Type-1 runs only on smartphones; Type-2 runs on supercomputers
Type-1 is written in Java; Type-2 is written in C
Type-1 has no virtual machines

explanation: Type-1 hypervisors (e.g., VMware ESXi, Xen, KVM) execute directly on server hardware. Type-2 hypervisors (e.g., VirtualBox, VMware Workstation) run within a conventional host OS.

prompt: What is Containerization (e.g., Docker, LXC) compared to traditional Virtual Machines?

options.text: OS-level virtualization that shares the host OS kernel and isolates processes, offering much lower overhead than full VMs
Emulation of hardware using software ALUs
Compressing files into containerized archives
Running code inside physical metal containers

explanation: Containers isolate user spaces using kernel namespaces and cgroups while sharing the single underlying host kernel, avoiding the heavy memory overhead of running separate guest OS kernels.

prompt: What is a 'Message Passing' IPC model in operating system design?

options.text: Processes exchange information by sending packets/messages through the OS kernel via system calls (send, receive)
Processes directly read and write to the same shared physical memory RAM addresses
Users print documents and read them manually
Programs execute sequentially on a single thread

explanation: In message passing, communicating processes rely on kernel-mediated primitives (send, receive) without requiring shared address space, which is especially useful in distributed systems.

prompt: What is the primary advantage of the 'Shared Memory' IPC model over Message Passing?

options.text: High speed: once the shared segment is mapped, communication occurs at memory hardware speeds without kernel intervention
No synchronization is ever required between processes
It works automatically across separate networked computers without network cards
It prevents race conditions automatically

explanation: Shared memory allows processes to communicate directly by reading and writing to shared RAM, bypassing system call overhead during data transfer.

prompt: Which file format is the standard executable binary format used by Linux operating systems?

options.text: ELF (Executable and Linkable Format)
PE (Portable Executable)
COFF (Common Object File Format)
Mach-O

explanation: Linux uses ELF for object files, shared libraries, and executables. Windows uses PE (Portable Executable), and macOS uses Mach-O.

prompt: What is the 'init' (or systemd) process in UNIX/Linux systems?

options.text: The ancestor (PID 1) of all processes, spawned directly by the kernel at the end of the boot sequence
The text editor used to write scripts
The compiler for kernel modules
The background garbage collector for RAM

explanation: PID 1 (traditionally 'init', now 'systemd' in modern Linux) is the first user-space process initialized by the kernel, responsible for launching all daemons and user sessions.

prompt: What is an 'orphan process' in operating systems?

options.text: A running process whose parent process has terminated without waiting for it
A process that has no lines of code
A process that cannot be killed by SIGKILL
A process that has finished execution but remains in the process table

explanation: When a parent terminates before its child, the child becomes an orphan and is automatically adopted by PID 1 (init/systemd), which periodically reaps its exit status.

prompt: What is a 'zombie process' (defunct process)?

options.text: A process that has completed execution via exit(), but whose entry remains in the process table until its parent reads its exit status via wait()
A malicious virus that attacks the bootloader
A process that consumes 100% of CPU time indefinitely
A process running on a detached monitor

explanation: A zombie process has released its memory and open files but retains an entry in the process table with its termination code until its parent invokes wait().

prompt: What is the fundamental distinction between a 'Program' and a 'Process'?

options.text: A program is a passive entity (stored executable file on disk); a process is an active entity (a program in execution with PC, stack, and data)
A program can run on multiple computers; a process cannot
A program is stored in RAM; a process is stored in ROM
There is no distinction in computer science

explanation: A program is passive code stored on storage media. A process is an active executing instance possessing a program counter, memory segments, CPU registers, and resource handles.

prompt: What are the standard memory segments of an active process in virtual memory?

options.text: Text (Code), Data (Initialized globals), BSS (Uninitialized globals), Heap (Dynamic memory), Stack (Local variables, call frames)
Only RAM and Cache
Only BIOS and ROM
Only CPU registers and disk swap

explanation: A process memory layout comprises: Text (machine code), Data/BSS (global/static variables), Heap (dynamically allocated via malloc/new, growing upward), and Stack (function activation frames, growing downward).

prompt: What are the five states in the classic 5-State Process Model?

options.text: New, Ready, Running, Waiting (Blocked), Terminated
Start, Execute, Stop, Pause, Delete
Idle, Active, Sleeping, Suspended, Dead
Created, Swapped, Paged, Cached, Cleared

explanation: The 5-state lifecycle consists of: New (being created), Ready (waiting in ready queue for CPU), Running (instructions executing on CPU), Waiting (blocked waiting for I/O or event), and Terminated (finished).

prompt: What transition occurs when a running process requires an I/O operation?

options.text: Running -> Waiting (Blocked)
Running -> Ready
Running -> Terminated
Waiting -> Running

explanation: When an active process issues an I/O request or waits for an event, it voluntarily relinquishes the CPU and transitions from Running to Waiting.

prompt: What transition occurs when an operating system timer interrupt expires on a running process in preemptive scheduling?

options.text: Running -> Ready
Running -> Waiting
Running -> Terminated
Ready -> Running

explanation: When a running process exhausts its time slice, the OS timer interrupt preempts it, transitioning it back to the Ready queue to await its next turn.

prompt: What data structure does the Operating System maintain to track all state and accounting information for each individual process?

options.text: Process Control Block (PCB) / Task Struct
Interrupt Vector Table
File Allocation Table
Page Directory Pointer Table

explanation: The PCB (Task Descriptor) stores Process ID (PID), program counter, CPU registers, scheduling priority, memory management pointers, accounting data, and I/O status info.

prompt: What is a 'Context Switch' in operating systems?

options.text: Saving the CPU hardware state (registers, PC) of the currently running process and restoring the saved state of another process to resume execution
Switching from light mode to dark mode in the UI
Changing the network IP address of the system
Replacing physical RAM with virtual memory

explanation: Context switching saves the execution context of the active process into its PCB and loads the context of the newly scheduled process from its PCB.

prompt: Why is Context Switching considered pure computational overhead?

options.text: Because the CPU performs no productive user work while switching between processes
Because it permanently deletes CPU cache data
Because it causes hardware damage to transistors
Because it slows down typing speed

explanation: During a context switch, the OS consumes CPU cycles saving registers, updating pointers, and invalidating memory caches, during which no user instructions advance.

prompt: What is the primary role of the 'Short-Term Scheduler' (CPU Scheduler)?

options.text: Selects which process from the Ready Queue should be allocated the CPU next for execution
Selects which jobs should be brought from disk into memory
Swaps processes between RAM and disk
Controls the screen refresh rate

explanation: The Short-Term Scheduler executes very frequently (e.g., every 10-100 ms), picking the next process from the ready queue to dispatch to the CPU.

prompt: What is the primary role of the 'Long-Term Scheduler' (Job Scheduler)?

options.text: Controls the degree of multiprogramming by selecting which batch jobs from disk are admitted into main memory
Selects which thread runs on the ALU next
Handles keyboard button press interrupts
Manages page replacements in cache

explanation: The Long-Term Scheduler determines which submitted jobs enter the system, regulating the total number of processes residing in main memory (degree of multiprogramming).

prompt: What is the role of the 'Medium-Term Scheduler'?

options.text: Swaps processes out of main memory to disk (backing store) to reduce the degree of multiprogramming and free RAM
Schedules disk head movements
Controls mouse cursor acceleration
Cleans cache files on shutdown

explanation: The Medium-Term Scheduler implements swapping: when memory becomes congested, it swaps suspended processes out to disk and later swaps them back in when resources free up.

prompt: What is the difference between an 'I/O-Bound' process and a 'CPU-Bound' process?

options.text: An I/O-bound process spends more time doing I/O than computations, having many short CPU bursts; a CPU-bound process generates few long CPU bursts
An I/O-bound process never uses the CPU
A CPU-bound process cannot access the hard drive
An I/O-bound process runs only on GPUs

explanation: I/O-bound processes execute brief CPU computations before blocking for I/O. CPU-bound processes spend the vast majority of their lifespan executing intensive arithmetic calculations.

prompt: What is a 'Thread' (Light-Weight Process)?

options.text: A basic unit of CPU execution within a process, having its own program counter, register set, and stack, but sharing the text and data segments with sibling threads
A separate standalone operating system running inside a window
A physical cable connecting CPU to RAM
A hardware timer circuit

explanation: A thread is the smallest schedulable entity. All threads of a process share the same address space (code, global data, open files) while maintaining independent stacks and execution contexts.

prompt: Which of the following resources is NOT shared among threads of the same process?

options.text: Stack and CPU Registers (Program Counter)
Heap Memory
Global Variables and Data Segment
Open File Descriptors

explanation: Each thread has its own private execution stack (local variables, return addresses) and register state. The heap, data, text, and file descriptors are shared by all threads of that process.

prompt: What is the 'Many-to-One' multithreading model?

options.text: Multiple user-level threads are mapped to a single kernel thread
Multiple kernel threads run on a single CPU core
One user thread controls multiple hardware monitors
A thread with multiple return statements

explanation: In Many-to-One (user-level threading), thread management is done in user space without kernel awareness. If one thread makes a blocking system call, the entire process blocks.

prompt: What is the 'One-to-One' multithreading model (standard in Linux and Windows)?

options.text: Each user-level thread maps directly to an independent kernel thread
One process can only contain one thread
One CPU can only execute one instruction per second
Threads cannot access shared memory

explanation: In One-to-One model, the OS kernel manages each thread directly. If one thread blocks, other threads continue executing concurrently on multi-core CPUs.

prompt: What is the definition of 'Throughput' in CPU scheduling?

options.text: The number of processes completed per unit of time
The total time a process spends waiting in the ready queue
The time from process submission to its complete termination
The percentage of time the CPU is busy

explanation: Throughput measures the overall productivity of the scheduling system: count of completed processes per hour or minute.

prompt: What is 'Turnaround Time' in CPU scheduling?

options.text: The total elapsed time interval from the instant a process is submitted to its complete termination
The time the process spends executing on the CPU only
The time taken to switch context between two threads
The time spent waiting for the first response

explanation: Turnaround Time = Completion Time - Arrival Time. It includes time spent waiting for memory admission, ready queue waiting, CPU execution, and I/O operations.

prompt: What is 'Waiting Time' in CPU scheduling?

options.text: The total time a process spends waiting in the Ready Queue to gain access to the CPU
The time the process spends sleeping on disk
The time taken for a printer to output paper
The duration of the CPU burst

explanation: Waiting Time = Turnaround Time - Burst Time. It reflects how long the process sat idle in the ready queue.

prompt: What is 'Response Time' in CPU scheduling?

options.text: The time elapsed from the submission of a request until the first output response is produced
The time taken to shut down the operating system
The total execution time of the entire batch
The time between two consecutive keypresses

explanation: Response time is crucial in interactive systems: it measures the latency before the user receives the first sign of system reaction to an input.

prompt: What is the 'Convoy Effect' observed in First-Come, First-Served (FCFS) scheduling?

options.text: Short processes get stuck waiting behind a long, CPU-intensive process, causing overall device utilization and average waiting time to suffer
Multiple threads competing for the same lock
A network packet storm saturating the ethernet card
Context switches occurring too quickly in Round Robin

explanation: In non-preemptive FCFS, if a large CPU-burst job arrives first, all subsequent short I/O-bound jobs queue behind it, resulting in poor average wait times (the Convoy Effect).

prompt: Which CPU scheduling algorithm gives the mathematically minimum theoretical average waiting time for a given set of stationary processes?

options.text: Shortest Job First (SJF) Scheduling
First-Come, First-Served (FCFS)
Round Robin (RR)
Priority Scheduling without aging

explanation: SJF is provably optimal in terms of minimizing average waiting time because moving short jobs to the front reduces waiting time for all subsequent jobs.

prompt: What is the preemptive version of Shortest Job First (SJF) scheduling called?

options.text: Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF)
First In First Out (FIFO)
Round Robin (RR)
Multilevel Queue

explanation: In SRTF, if a new process arrives with a remaining CPU burst shorter than the remaining burst of the currently running process, the running process is preempted.

prompt: What is the primary practical difficulty in implementing Shortest Job First (SJF) scheduling in general-purpose OS kernels?

options.text: It is impossible to know the exact length of the next CPU burst of a process in advance
Modern CPUs do not support sorting algorithms
SJF requires infinite memory
SJF only works with single-character process names

explanation: The Linux kernel OOM Killer algorithm computes an oom_badness score and issues SIGKILL to high-impact sacrifice processes to reclaim free memory.

prompt: What is 'Shared Memory Architecture' using Paging?

options.text: Two or more processes map the same physical frame into their respective page tables, allowing instant zero-copy data exchange
Connecting two PCs with a LAN cable
Using two monitors on one computer
Writing data to a shared DVD

explanation: By pointing entries in different process page tables to the same physical frame, both processes share the underlying physical RAM without duplication.

prompt: What is a 'Semaphore' as defined by Edsger Dijkstra?

options.text: A protected integer variable S accessed only through two standard atomic operations: wait() [P] and signal() [V]
A hardware switch on the front panel of mainframes
A network routing protocol
A data encryption key

explanation: A semaphore is a synchronization primitive consisting of an integer counter manipulated exclusively by atomic operations wait() (decrement) and signal() (increment).

prompt: What is the atomic definition of the wait() [or P()] operation on semaphore S?

options.text: wait(S): while (S <= 0) { busy wait or block }; S--;
wait(S): S++;
wait(S): S = 0;
wait(S): return S;

explanation: wait(S) tests if S > 0; if not, the calling process waits or sleeps. Once S > 0, it decrements S atomically.

prompt: What is the atomic definition of the signal() [or V()] operation on semaphore S?

options.text: signal(S): S++; (and wakes up a waiting process, if any)
signal(S): S--;
signal(S): while (S > 0) sleep;
signal(S): S = -1;

explanation: signal(S) atomically increments the semaphore value S and unblocks any waiting thread suspended in the semaphore queue.

prompt: What is a 'Binary Semaphore'?

options.text: A semaphore whose integer value can only range between 0 and 1, used as a Mutual Exclusion Lock (Mutex)
A semaphore that can only take powers of 2
A semaphore stored in binary file format
A semaphore for 2-bit microcontrollers

explanation: A binary semaphore is restricted to values 0 and 1, functioning identically to a mutex lock.

prompt: What is a 'Counting Semaphore'?

options.text: A semaphore whose value can span an unrestricted integer domain, used to manage access to a finite pool of identical resource instances
A timer that counts seconds
A process counter in the taskbar
A counter for network packets

explanation: Counting semaphores are initialized to the number of available resource instances; each allocation decrements the count, and release increments it.

prompt: In the classic Producer-Consumer Problem with a bounded buffer of size N, which semaphores are typically used?

options.text: mutex (initialized to 1), empty (initialized to N), and full (initialized to 0)
Only a single boolean flag
Three integer arrays
No semaphores are needed

explanation: Standard solution: 'mutex' provides mutual exclusion for buffer insertion/removal; 'empty' counts vacant slots (init N); 'full' counts occupied slots (init 0).

prompt: In the Readers-Writers problem, what is the primary concurrency rule?

options.text: Multiple readers can read concurrently, but a writer requires exclusive access (no other readers or writers)
Only one reader can read at a time
Writers can write concurrently without locks
Readers and writers execute simultaneously

explanation: Shared data can safely be read by any number of concurrent readers, but writing requires exclusive mutual exclusion to prevent data corruption.

prompt: In the Dining Philosophers Problem, how can deadlock among 5 philosophers seated at a round table be prevented?

options.text: Allow at most 4 philosophers to sit at the table simultaneously, or make odd philosophers pick left fork first and even philosophers pick right fork first
Remove all forks from the table
Let all philosophers eat at the exact same second
Increase the number of philosophers to 10

explanation: Asymmetric chopstick acquisition (odd/even ordering) or limiting seating capacity to N-1 breaks the circular wait condition, guaranteeing deadlock-free execution.

prompt: What is a 'Monitor' in concurrent programming (e.g., in Java synchronized methods)?

options.text: A high-level language synchronization construct encapsulating shared variables, functions, and condition variables, guaranteeing that only one thread executes inside the monitor at any time
A physical display screen
A background thread that watches CPU temperatures
A hardware logic analyzer

explanation: Monitors provide automated compiler-enforced mutual exclusion: only one active thread can execute within a monitor procedure at any given instant.

prompt: What are the two primitive operations supported on a 'Condition Variable' inside a Monitor?

options.text: wait() and signal()
lock() and unlock()
push() and pop()
start() and stop()

explanation: Condition variables provide signaling mechanisms inside monitors: x.wait() suspends the invoking thread until another thread calls x.signal().

prompt: What is a 'Deadlock' in an operating system?

options.text: A situation where every process in a set is waiting for an event (resource release) that can only be caused by another process in the same set, resulting in permanent stagnation
A computer that cannot boot due to dead battery
A process that terminates with error code 1
An encrypted file with lost password

explanation: Deadlock is a circular freeze where multiple processes hold resources while waiting for resources held by others in the loop, bringing all of them to an indefinite halt.

prompt: What are the FOUR necessary conditions that must hold simultaneously for a Deadlock to occur (Coffman Conditions)?

options.text: Mutual Exclusion, Hold and Wait, No Preemption, Circular Wait
Speed, Priority, Capacity, Quantum
Read, Write, Execute, Delete
CPU, RAM, Disk, Network

explanation: E. G. Coffman proved in 1971 that deadlock requires all 4 conditions: 1. Mutual Exclusion, 2. Hold and Wait, 3. No Preemption, and 4. Circular Wait.

prompt: What does the 'Hold and Wait' condition mean in deadlock theory?

options.text: A process currently holding at least one allocated resource is actively waiting to acquire additional resources held by other processes
A process is paused by the user
The CPU holds instructions in cache
A printer holds paper in tray

explanation: Hold and wait means processes do not release their currently held resources while blocking to request more resources.

prompt: What does the 'No Preemption' condition mean?

options.text: Resources cannot be forcibly confiscated from a process; they can only be released voluntarily by the process holding them after task completion
Processes cannot be interrupted by the timer
The CPU cannot run threads
Memory cannot be expanded

explanation: No preemption means allocated resources are sacrosanct and cannot be preempted by the OS kernel without the owner's cooperation.

prompt: What does the 'Circular Wait' condition mean?

options.text: A closed chain of processes exists: P0 waits for P1, P1 waits for P2, ..., Pn waits for P0
A thread executing a while(true) loop
A circular hard drive platter rotating
A round-robin ready queue

explanation: Circular wait is the definitive topological loop of dependency where each process in the chain waits for a resource held by the next member.

prompt: In a Resource Allocation Graph (RAG), what does a directed edge from Process P_i to Resource R_j (P_i -> R_j) signify?

options.text: Request Edge (Process P_i has requested an instance of resource R_j and is waiting)
Assignment Edge (Resource R_j is allocated to P_i)
Process creation edge
Data transfer edge

explanation: P_i -> R_j is a Request Edge. Conversely, R_j -> P_i is an Assignment Edge indicating that an instance of R_j is held by P_i.

prompt: In a Resource Allocation Graph, what does a cycle indicate if each resource type has ONLY ONE single instance?

options.text: A cycle is necessary and sufficient condition for Deadlock (Deadlock definitely exists)
Deadlock may or may not exist
The system is guaranteed safe
The computer will reboot

explanation: If all resources have single instances, a graph cycle is both necessary and sufficient for deadlock: a cycle implies an active deadlock.

prompt: In a Resource Allocation Graph, what does a cycle indicate if resource types have MULTIPLE instances?

options.text: A cycle is a necessary condition, but NOT a sufficient condition for deadlock (Deadlock MAY exist)
Deadlock is guaranteed to exist
No deadlock can ever exist
The graph is invalid

explanation: With multi-instance resources, a cycle does not guarantee deadlock because processes outside the cycle could release instances to break the wait.

prompt: What are the three general strategies for handling Deadlocks in operating systems?

options.text: Deadlock Prevention, Deadlock Avoidance, and Deadlock Detection & Recovery (plus the Ostrich algorithm)
Rebooting every 5 minutes
Disabling multi-threading
Allocating infinite memory

explanation: The 3 formal strategies are Prevention (structural elimination of Coffman conditions), Avoidance (dynamic safety checking like Banker's), and Detection/Recovery (letting it happen, detecting it, and rolling back).

prompt: What is the 'Ostrich Algorithm' for handling deadlocks (used by general-purpose OSs like Linux and Windows)?

options.text: Stick your head in the sand and pretend deadlocks never occur; if one happens, rely on the user or admin to kill the frozen process
An algorithm developed in Australia
A machine learning neural network
A fast disk sorting algorithm

explanation: Because formal deadlock handling incurs heavy runtime overhead, general-purpose OSs ignore deadlocks under the economic trade-off that they occur rarely.

prompt: How does Deadlock Prevention eliminate the 'Circular Wait' condition?

options.text: Impose a strict global linear ordering (enumeration) on all resource types, requiring processes to request resources only in strictly increasing order
Allow all processes to run in parallel
Disable all locks
Make all resources infinite

explanation: By Havender's protocol, if resources are numbered 1..K and every process must request resources in strictly monotonically increasing numerical order, a cyclic dependency chain is mathematically impossible.

prompt: How does Deadlock Prevention eliminate the 'Hold and Wait' condition?

options.text: Require a process to request and receive ALL required resources at once before beginning execution, or release all held resources before requesting more
Kill all processes after 10 seconds
Give CPU to only one process forever
Make all processes hold zero variables

explanation: Protocol requires atomic upfront allocation of all resources, preventing a process from holding some while waiting for others (sacrifices resource utilization).

prompt: What is a 'Safe State' in Deadlock Avoidance theory?

options.text: A state where there exists at least one Safe Sequence <P1, P2, ..., Pn> such that every process can finish using currently available resources plus resources held by prior processes
A state where the computer is turned off
A state where all files are encrypted
A state with no network connection

explanation: A safe state guarantees that the OS can allocate resources to satisfy maximum claims without deadlocking.

prompt: What is the fundamental relationship between a Safe State, an Unsafe State, and a Deadlock?

options.text: A safe state is NOT deadlock; an unsafe state MAY lead to deadlock; deadlock is a subset of unsafe states
Unsafe state and deadlock are identical
All safe states are deadlocked
Deadlock has no relation to safe states

explanation: An unsafe state is not necessarily deadlocked; rather, it is a vulnerable state where unfavorable process claims can force the system into deadlock.

prompt: Who invented the famous 'Banker's Algorithm' for Deadlock Avoidance?

options.text: Edsger W. Dijkstra
Alan Turing
John von Neumann
Dennis Ritchie

explanation: Dijkstra designed the Banker's Algorithm in 1965, modeled after a small-town banker managing lines of cash credit.

prompt: What are the primary data structures maintained by the Banker's Algorithm for n processes and m resource types?

options.text: Available[m], Max[n, m], Allocation[n, m], and Need[n, m]
Queue, Stack, Linked List, Tree
PID, PC, Registers, Stack Pointer
Rows, Columns, Cells, Formulas

explanation: Available tracks free instances; Max tracks maximum declared demand; Allocation tracks currently held instances; Need = Max - Allocation tracks remaining claims.

prompt: What is the formula to calculate the Need matrix in the Banker's Algorithm?

options.text: Need[i, j] = Max[i, j] - Allocation[i, j]
Need[i, j] = Max[i, j] + Allocation[i, j]
Need[i, j] = Available[j] - Allocation[i, j]
Need[i, j] = Allocation[i, j] / Max[i, j]

explanation: Remaining Need for process i of resource j is its peak demand minus what it already holds: Need = Max - Allocation.

prompt: Under the Resource-Request Algorithm of the Banker's method, what check must pass before a request from P_i can even be evaluated for safety?

options.text: Request_i <= Need_i AND Request_i <= Available
Request_i > Max_i
Request_i == 0
Allocation_i == Max_i

explanation: If Request > Need, an error is raised (exceeding maximum declared claim). If Request > Available, the process must wait due to lack of resources.

prompt: In Deadlock Detection with single-instance resource types, what graph reduction structure is used?

options.text: Wait-For Graph (WFG) obtained by removing resource nodes and collapsing edges directly between processes
Binary Search Tree
Spanning Forest
B-Tree

explanation: A Wait-For Graph contains only process nodes: edge P_i -> P_j means P_i is waiting for P_j to release a resource. A cycle in WFG indicates deadlock.

prompt: What are the standard recovery techniques when an OS Deadlock Detection algorithm discovers a deadlock?

options.text: Process Termination (abort all or abort one-by-one) or Resource Preemption with Process Rollback to a safe checkpoint
Deleting the hard drive partition
Disabling CPU interrupts
Running an antivirus scan

explanation: The OS recovers by terminating deadlocked processes until the cycle breaks, or preempting resources from victim processes and rolling them back to saved checkpoints.

prompt: What factor is critical when selecting a 'victim' process for preemption during deadlock recovery?

options.text: Minimizing cost (process priority, CPU time consumed so far, resources held, and whether interactive or batch)
Killing the oldest process always
Killing the process with the shortest name
Random selection

explanation: Victim selection weighs: CPU time already spent, resources held, remaining completion time, and process priority to minimize wasted compute.

prompt: What is 'Starvation' in the context of Deadlock Recovery via preemption?

options.text: The same unfortunate process is repeatedly chosen as the preemption victim and never gets to complete its work
The CPU runs out of electrical power
A file system running out of disk inodes
A process with no variables

explanation: If cost metrics are static, the same process may be preempted repeatedly. Solutions include factoring the number of past preemptions into the cost function.

prompt: What is a 'Livelock'?

options.text: Two or more processes continuously change their states in response to each other without making any forward progress (active busy-waiting stalemate)
A permanent hardware lockup
A process that cannot be killed by task manager
A deadlocked thread that has finished

explanation: Unlike deadlock where threads sleep, livelocked threads are actively running and consuming CPU, but repeatedly react to each other in an infinite dance without advancing.

prompt: What is 'Priority Inversion' in concurrent real-time operating systems?

options.text: A high-priority process is indirectly blocked by a low-priority process holding a shared lock, because a medium-priority process preempts the low-priority process
A bug where high priority is treated as zero
A priority queue sorted in reverse
A thread that refuses to yield the CPU

explanation: Priority inversion occurred famously on the Mars Pathfinder spacecraft: low-priority task held a mutex, medium tasks starved it from finishing, indirectly blocking the urgent high-priority task.

prompt: What classic protocol solves the Priority Inversion problem in real-time operating systems?

options.text: Priority Inheritance Protocol (the low-priority process holding the lock temporarily inherits the high priority of the blocked process)
Round Robin scheduling with 1 ms quantum
Disabling all priority queues
Terminating all medium tasks immediately

explanation: Under priority inheritance, whichever task holds a lock needed by a higher-priority task temporarily runs at that higher priority until it releases the lock.

prompt: In the Banker's Algorithm, if System State has Available = [3, 3, 2], and P0 needs [0, 0, 0], can P0 be added to the safe sequence?

options.text: Yes, because Need <= Available, so P0 can finish and release its allocated resources to Available
No, P0 must wait
Only if P0 is the only process
Cannot be determined

explanation: If Need <= Available, the process can safely obtain its peak resources, complete execution, and return its entire allocation back to the available pool.

prompt: What is a 'Spinlock with Backoff' designed to alleviate?

options.text: Memory bus contention and cache coherence traffic caused by multiple CPU cores hammering the same atomic memory address
Hard drive head seek delays
Network bandwidth throttling
Keyboard typing latency

explanation: Exponential backoff delays successive spinlock checks when contention is high, reducing memory bus saturation across CPU sockets.

prompt: What is the difference between a 'Recursive Mutex' (Reentrant Lock) and a standard Mutex?

options.text: A recursive mutex allows the thread currently holding the lock to acquire it multiple times without deadlocking itself
A recursive mutex can be unlocked by any thread
A recursive mutex only works inside recursive functions
A recursive mutex is written in C++

explanation: A reentrant lock tracks acquisition depth; the owning thread can re-lock it without self-deadlock, provided it unlocks an equal number of times.

prompt: What does POSIX pthread_mutex_lock() do if the mutex is already locked by another thread?

options.text: Puts the calling thread to sleep (blocks) until the mutex is released and the thread is awakened
Returns immediately with an error code
Terminates the calling thread
Spins at 100% CPU forever

explanation: pthread_mutex_lock blocks the calling thread, placing it in a wait queue so no CPU cycles are wasted while waiting.

prompt: What does POSIX pthread_mutex_trylock() do?

options.text: Attempts to acquire the lock; if already held, it returns immediately with EBUSY without blocking
Blocks indefinitely until lock is acquired
Forces the other thread to release the lock
Destroys the mutex

explanation: trylock() provides a non-blocking poll mechanism, allowing threads to avoid deadlock by performing other work if the lock is contested.

prompt: What are the ACID properties guaranteed by transaction processing in database and OS storage systems?

options.text: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability
Authentication, Compression, Indexing, and Deletion
Asynchronous, Concurrent, Iterative, and Distributed
Allocation, Compaction, Interleaving, and Defragmentation

explanation: ACID guarantees transactional reliability: Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (preserves invariants), Isolation (concurrent transactions don't interfere), Durability (committed writes persist across crashes).

prompt: What does the 'Atomicity' property of an operation mean?

options.text: The operation executes completely as a single indivisible unit, or if any part fails, the entire operation is rolled back with no partial effects
The operation runs on atomic particles
The operation takes 1 nanosecond
The operation cannot be logged

explanation: Atomicity ensures operations are 'all-or-nothing', preventing partially completed corrupt states.

prompt: How do blocking semaphores eliminate the 'Busy Waiting' (CPU spinning) present in spinlocks?

options.text: When a process finds S <= 0, it places itself on the semaphore's waiting queue and invokes block() to yield the CPU to other processes
By increasing the clock speed
By terminating the process immediately
By converting the semaphore to a float

explanation: Blocking semaphores suspend the waiting process in a sleep queue, letting the scheduler run other productive tasks until signal() invokes wakeup().

prompt: In UNIX System V IPC, which family of system calls is used to create and operate on semaphore sets?

options.text: semget(), semop(), and semctl()
fork(), exec(), wait()
pipe(), dup(), read()
socket(), bind(), listen()

explanation: System V semaphore API uses semget() to create/access a semaphore set, semop() to perform atomic increment/decrement operations, and semctl() for control and initialization.

prompt: What is the fundamental difference between 'Deadlock' and 'Starvation'?

options.text: In deadlock, every involved process is blocked indefinitely and none can proceed; in starvation, some processes make continuous progress while one or more unfortunate processes are starved
Deadlock only occurs on single-core CPUs; starvation occurs on multi-core
Deadlock resolves itself automatically; starvation never resolves
There is no difference

explanation: In starvation, the system as a whole advances, but an individual process is unfairly bypassed. In deadlock, the entire set of processes is completely frozen with zero system progress.

prompt: What is the computational time complexity of running the Banker's Algorithm Safety Check for n processes and m resource types?

options.text: O(n + m)
O(m^n)

explanation: Finding a safe sequence requires checking at most n processes across n iterations, where each step tests m resource instances, giving a time complexity of O(m * n^2).

prompt: What is 'Checkpointing' in system fault tolerance and deadlock recovery?

options.text: Periodically saving the complete execution state (registers, memory) of a process to non-volatile storage to allow rollback to that known safe state
Checking the hard drive for viruses
Marking code lines with comments
Pausing a process during debugging

explanation: Checkpoints provide recovery milestones, ensuring that if resource preemption is required, a victim process does not need to restart from the very beginning.

prompt: What is 'False Sharing' in concurrent multi-threaded programming on multi-core CPUs?

options.text: Threads on different cores modify independent variables that reside on the exact same 64-byte hardware cache line, causing unnecessary cache invalidation traffic
Sharing passwords across users
Threads reading wrong memory addresses
Using shared memory without permissions

explanation: False sharing occurs when independent variables share a single cache line; modifying one variable causes the cache hardware to invalidate the entire line on all other cores, degrading performance.

prompt: What does the 'Circular Wait' condition require in terms of resource types?

options.text: Each process in the chain must be waiting for a resource that is held by the subsequent process in the cycle
All resources must be of the same type
Resources must be allocated in alphabetical order
Processes must be running in Round Robin order

explanation: Circular wait is the definitive topological loop of dependency where each process in the chain waits for a resource held by the next member.

prompt: What is a 'Futex' (Fast Userspace Mutex) in the Linux kernel?

options.text: A synchronization construct that attempts lock acquisition in user space via atomic instructions and calls into the kernel only if contention occurs
A lock for flash drives
A fast thread scheduling queue
A future execution promise

explanation: Futex optimizes lock performance by executing uncontended lock/unlock operations in user space with zero system call overhead, falling back to kernel sleeping only when contested.

The user's desktop folder
A software compiler for scripts

unit_title: File Systems, Secondary Storage Management & Disk Scheduling
prompt: What are the two primary components of physical disk access latency in traditional magnetic Hard Disk Drives (HDD)?

options.text: Seek Time (moving the R/W head to the target cylinder) and Rotational Latency (waiting for the target sector to rotate under the head)
Download speed and upload speed
CPU clock speed and bus speed
RAM refresh time and cache latency

explanation: Total disk latency is dominated by Seek Time (mechanical arm movement, 3-10 ms) and Rotational Delay (spinning platters, 2-6 ms).

unit_title: File Systems, Secondary Storage Management & Disk Scheduling
prompt: Why do Solid State Drives (SSDs) NOT require traditional disk head scheduling algorithms like SCAN or LOOK?

options.text: SSDs have no moving mechanical parts, providing uniform random access latency across all flash memory blocks
SSDs cannot store files
SSDs run in RAM only
SSDs use magnetic tapes

explanation: Because flash memory has zero mechanical seek time or rotational latency, algorithms designed to minimize head travel distance are irrelevant for SSDs.

unit_title: File Systems, Secondary Storage Management & Disk Scheduling
prompt: What is the primary operational goal of Disk Head Scheduling algorithms in HDDs?

options.text: To minimize total head movement (seek distance) and average seek time across all I/O cylinder requests
To make the disk spin faster
To compress video files on the fly
To increase the sector size

explanation: Minimizing mechanical head travel distance maximizes throughput and minimizes request queue wait time.

unit_title: File Systems, Secondary Storage Management & Disk Scheduling
prompt: How does the First-Come, First-Served (FCFS) disk scheduling algorithm operate?

options.text: Services requests strictly in the chronological order they arrive in the I/O queue, without considering head location
Services the closest cylinder first
Services requests in alphabetical order
Sweeps back and forth across platters

explanation: FCFS is intrinsically fair with no starvation risk, but can cause wild head oscillations across the disk surface, resulting in poor performance.

unit_title: File Systems, Secondary Storage Management & Disk Scheduling
prompt: What is the Shortest Seek Time First (SSTF) disk scheduling algorithm?

options.text: Selects the pending request that requires the least head movement from the current cylinder position
Services the shortest file first
Services the request with the highest PID
Moves head to cylinder 0 first

explanation: SSTF picks the geometrically closest track to the current head, substantially reducing total seek distance compared to FCFS.

unit_title: File Systems, Secondary Storage Management & Disk Scheduling
prompt: What major drawback does SSTF disk scheduling suffer from?

options.text: Starvation of outlying requests if a steady stream of requests keeps arriving near the current head position
It requires infinite memory
It causes mechanical arm collisions
It can only handle 10 requests at a time

explanation: Just like SJF in CPU scheduling, SSTF can permanently starve requests for distant inner or outer cylinders if local requests continuously arrive.

unit_title: File Systems, Secondary Storage Management & Disk Scheduling
prompt: How does the SCAN (Elevator) disk scheduling algorithm operate?

options.text: The disk arm starts at one end and moves toward the other end, servicing requests along the way, until it reaches the edge, where it reverses direction
It moves directly to the center and stops
It jumps randomly between requests
It services requests based on file size

explanation: Like a building elevator, SCAN sweeps in one direction until it hits the physical disk boundary, then reverses direction, guaranteeing bounded wait times.

unit_title: File Systems, Secondary Storage Management & Disk Scheduling
prompt: How does C-SCAN (Circular SCAN) disk scheduling improve upon standard SCAN?

options.text: It moves in one direction only servicing requests; when it reaches the edge, it immediately returns to the beginning WITHOUT servicing requests on the return trip
It spins the disk platters backwards
It services requests in a circular spiral
It doubles the disk head speed

explanation: C-SCAN provides a more uniform waiting time distribution because requests at the far end do not wait twice as long as requests in the middle.

unit_title: File Systems, Secondary Storage Management & Disk Scheduling
prompt: How does the LOOK disk scheduling algorithm optimize the standard SCAN algorithm?

options.text: The arm goes only as far as the final pending request in each direction, reversing direction immediately without traveling to the physical end of the disk
It checks file contents before moving
It predicts future user requests using AI
It looks at CPU temperature

explanation: LOOK checks ahead ('looks') and reverses direction as soon as no further requests exist in the current direction, avoiding unnecessary travel to platter edges.

unit_title: File Systems, Secondary Storage Management & Disk Scheduling
prompt: How does C-LOOK optimize C-SCAN?

options.text: The arm sweeps in one direction only as far as the last active request, then returns directly to the earliest pending request without going to the physical edges
It reads disk tracks circularly
It uses two read heads simultaneously
It writes data only to sector 0

explanation: C-LOOK restricts circular sweeps strictly between the lowest and highest active pending cylinder requests.

unit_title: File Systems, Secondary Storage Management & Disk Scheduling
prompt: Given a disk queue with requests for cylinders: 98, 183, 37, 122, 14, 124, 65, 67 with initial head at 53. If SSTF is used, which cylinder is serviced first?
explanation: Distances from 53: |65-53|=12, |37-53|=16, |67-53|=14. The minimum seek distance is 12, so cylinder 65 is serviced first.

unit_title: File Systems, Secondary Storage Management & Disk Scheduling
prompt: What is 'RAID' in secondary storage architecture?

options.text: Redundant Array of Independent (Inexpensive) Disks: organizing multiple physical disks to improve reliability, data redundancy, and I/O performance
A type of virus scanner
A disk partition format for games
A CPU instruction pipeline

explanation: RAID combines multiple physical hard drives into a single logical volume using striping, mirroring, or parity to boost throughput and fault tolerance.

unit_title: File Systems, Secondary Storage Management & Disk Scheduling
prompt: What is 'RAID 0' (Disk Striping)?

options.text: Data is split across multiple drives in blocks (stripes) with ZERO redundancy or parity; offers high performance but failure of any drive destroys all data
Data is mirrored across two drives
Parity is stored on a dedicated drive
Only one drive is used

explanation: RAID 0 offers non-redundant striping: peak read/write throughput, but zero fault tolerance.

unit_title: File Systems, Secondary Storage Management & Disk Scheduling
prompt: What is 'RAID 1' (Disk Mirroring)?

options.text: Every block of data written to one disk is simultaneously duplicated (mirrored) onto a second identical disk, providing 100% data redundancy
Striping with parity
Storing data on tape backups
Compressing files to half size

explanation: RAID 1 mirrors every sector onto a clone drive; if one disk crashes, the system continues seamlessly from the mirror.

unit_title: File Systems, Secondary Storage Management & Disk Scheduling
prompt: What is 'RAID 5' (Block-Interleaved Distributed Parity)?

options.text: Data and parity information are striped across three or more disks; can survive the complete loss of any single drive without data loss
Two disks mirrored together
All parity stored on a single drive
Ten disks running with no parity

explanation: RAID 5 requires at least 3 drives, distributing parity evenly across all drives so any single drive failure can be reconstructed via XOR parity.

unit_title: File Systems, Secondary Storage Management & Disk Scheduling
prompt: What is 'Journaling' in modern file systems (e.g., ext4, NTFS, XFS)?

options.text: Writing file system metadata changes to a circular log (journal) before committing them to the main file system structures, ensuring fast crash recovery
Keeping a diary of user logins
Writing text files with timestamps
Printing disk logs to paper

explanation: Journaling prevents file system inconsistency after power failure by replaying or rolling back unfinished operations from the journal on reboot, avoiding lengthy fsck scans.

unit_title: File Systems, Secondary Storage Management & Disk Scheduling
prompt: What is the 'Mounting' of a file system?

options.text: Attaching a file system on a storage device to a specified directory location (mount point) in the existing directory hierarchy
Physically screwing a hard drive into a computer chassis
Installing a cooling fan
Formatting a partition

explanation: Mounting links an external volume or partition into the unified OS directory tree at an accessible directory known as the mount point.

unit_title: File Systems, Secondary Storage Management & Disk Scheduling
prompt: What is a 'VFS' (Virtual File System) switch in the operating system kernel?

options.text: An abstraction layer that defines a common file interface (open, read, write) allowing the OS to access heterogeneous file systems (ext4, NTFS, NFS) uniformly
A virtual reality viewer
A hardware switch on SSDs
A tool for compressing folders

explanation: The VFS enables system calls like read() to function transparently whether the underlying target is on ext4, FAT32, Btrfs, or a network NFS drive.

unit_title: File Systems, Secondary Storage Management & Disk Scheduling
prompt: What is 'Bad Block Management' in disk controllers?

options.text: The disk controller detects damaged physical sectors and automatically remaps them to spare reserved sectors (sector sparing / forwarding)
Deleting all damaged files automatically
Disabling the entire hard drive
Turning off disk caching

explanation: Low-level controller firmware maintains a spare pool of sectors and transparently redirects reads and writes away from defective sectors.

unit_title: File Systems, Secondary Storage Management & Disk Scheduling
prompt: What is a 'Swap Space' on secondary storage?

options.text: A dedicated disk partition or file used by the virtual memory manager to hold pages that exceed physical RAM capacity
A folder for sharing files between users
A folder for temporary downloads
A recycle bin for deleted files

explanation: Swap space extends physical memory into non-volatile storage, holding evicted pages and hibernated system state.

unit_title: File Systems, Secondary Storage Management & Disk Scheduling
prompt: What is the difference between synchronous I/O and asynchronous I/O?

options.text: In synchronous I/O, the calling thread blocks until the I/O transfer completes; in asynchronous I/O, the thread continues executing while I/O proceeds in background
Synchronous I/O uses no wires
Asynchronous I/O can only write, never read
There is no difference

explanation: Asynchronous I/O invokes a signal or callback upon completion, allowing high-performance event-driven servers to service thousands of connections concurrently.

unit_title: File Systems, Secondary Storage Management & Disk Scheduling
prompt: What is Direct Memory Access (DMA)?

options.text: A specialized hardware controller that transfers blocks of data directly between I/O devices and main RAM without passing through the CPU
A CPU instruction that deletes RAM
A cable connecting two memory slots
A software tool to speed up typing

explanation: DMA relieves the CPU from byte-by-byte transfer chores; the CPU initiates the transfer and receives a single interrupt only when the entire multi-kilobyte block has moved.

unit_title: File Systems, Secondary Storage Management & Disk Scheduling
prompt: What is 'Double Buffering' in I/O management?

options.text: Using two memory buffers so the operating system can read from one buffer while an I/O device is writing into the other
Using two monitors at the same time
Backing up a file twice
Compressing data with two passwords

explanation: Double buffering decouples device speed from processing speed, allowing continuous data pipelining without stalling.

unit_title: File Systems, Secondary Storage Management & Disk Scheduling
prompt: What is the primary difference between Character-Stream devices and Block devices?

options.text: Character devices transfer data byte-by-byte in streams (e.g., keyboard, serial port); Block devices transfer fixed-size blocks with random seek capability (e.g., HDD, SSD)
Character devices are faster than block devices
Block devices cannot store binary data
Character devices use no drivers

explanation: UNIX categorizes hardware drivers into block devices (random-access, buffered) and character devices (stream-oriented, unbuffered).

unit_title: File Systems, Secondary Storage Management & Disk Scheduling
prompt: What does the 'fsync()' system call do in UNIX/Linux?

options.text: Forces all modified in-core file buffers (dirty cache blocks) for a file descriptor to be flushed and written to physical storage media immediately
Synchronizes the system clock with GPS
Deletes temporary backup files
Synchronizes two git repositories

explanation: fsync() ensures database write-ahead logging (WAL) durability by blocking until all cached data is physically committed to non-volatile disk platters or flash cells.

unit_title: File Systems, Secondary Storage Management & Disk Scheduling
prompt: What is 'Page Cache' in Linux kernel memory management?

options.text: A unified kernel cache in RAM that buffers disk blocks and file pages, serving file reads and writes at RAM speed
A cache for web browser HTML pages
A hardware chip on hard drives
A table of deleted files

explanation: Linux uses all otherwise-free RAM as a Page Cache to accelerate disk I/O; cache pages are evicted automatically when user applications request more memory.

unit_title: File Systems, Secondary Storage Management & Disk Scheduling
prompt: What is 'Copy-on-Write' snapshotting in modern filesystems like ZFS and Btrfs?

options.text: Instead of overwriting existing data, new modifications are written to new free blocks, allowing instant, space-efficient filesystem snapshots
Copying files to external thumb drives
A copyright protection system
A printer spooling technique

explanation: CoW filesystems preserve historical tree roots, allowing zero-latency point-in-time snapshots that consume storage only when blocks diverge.

unit_title: File Systems, Secondary Storage Management & Disk Scheduling
prompt: What is 'Wear Leveling' in Solid State Drives (SSDs)?

options.text: An internal controller algorithm that distributes flash writes and erasures evenly across all physical flash memory blocks to prevent premature block burnout
A tool to measure battery degradation
A fan control system to reduce wear
A mechanical alignment for SATA plugs

explanation: NAND flash cells endure a finite number of Program/Erase (P/E) cycles; wear leveling prevents specific sectors from burning out ahead of the rest.

unit_title: File Systems, Secondary Storage Management & Disk Scheduling
prompt: What is the TRIM command in SSD management?

options.text: An OS ATA/NVMe command informing the SSD which data blocks are no longer considered in use by the filesystem and can be wiped internally
A command to delete empty directories
A tool to truncate long filenames
A power saving sleep mode

explanation: TRIM enables the SSD garbage collection engine to pre-erase freed flash blocks in the background, preserving high sustained write performance.

unit_title: File Systems, Secondary Storage Management & Disk Scheduling
prompt: Why are Operating Systems considered the cornerstone of modern computer science and software development?

options.text: They bridge the gap between abstract user algorithms and chaotic physical hardware, orchestrating concurrency, security, memory, and devices seamlessly
Because without an OS, computers cannot be sold in stores
Because programming languages cannot run on bare electricity
Because monitors require an operating system to display colors

explanation: Operating systems provide the core infrastructure of computing: resource virtualization, process orchestration, memory protection, persistent storage, and fault-tolerant security.
